summary:
TerraCity is an interactive Earth science application that helps users investigate climate patterns across locations and over time. We developed a research dashboard combining NASA POWER records for temperature, rainfall, solar radiation, humidity, and wind with natural-language queries, interactive maps, and statistical analysis. 

Users can compare cities, examine monthly and annual charts, draw study areas, and inspect individual grid cells. The app calculates trend estimates, significance, and uncertainty, while optional AI explanations help users interpret results. A guided Vietnam tutorial introduces the tools, and a searchable source directory connects findings to datasets and downloadable records.

TerraCity addresses the challenge of making complex Earth observation data accessible and understandable. It brings data retrieval, visualization, analysis, and source tracing into one workflow. This matters because students, researchers, and communities need accessible ways to explore environmental change, question assumptions, and communicate findings supported by evidence.
details:
TerraCity is a browser-based Earth science application that helps people investigate how climate conditions change across places and over time. It brings data retrieval, geographic exploration, visualization, statistical analysis, and source tracing into one workspace.

Users begin by selecting locations, climate variables, and a time period through dashboard controls or supported natural-language requests. The app retrieves monthly NASA POWER records for temperature, precipitation, solar radiation, relative humidity, and wind speed. It filters missing-value flags and measurements outside configured bounds, aligns observations by date, and calculates trend statistics.

The dashboard lets users compare locations, switch between monthly observations and annual averages, and inspect individual measurements. An interactive globe and world map provide geographic context. Users can also draw rectangular study areas and examine the returned grid cells through coverage tables, trend estimates, and monthly charts. Two-variable comparisons combine separate chart axes with Pearson and Spearman correlation.

Seasonal Mann–Kendall tests and Theil–Sen slope estimates help users examine trend direction, magnitude, significance, and uncertainty. Optional Gemini explanations translate calculated results into accessible language. Users can inspect the dashboard before requesting an AI explanation, giving them control over the workflow and API usage.

TerraCity benefits newcomers through a guided Vietnam tutorial that works with bundled observations without requiring a Gemini key. Its five activities introduce queries, chart interpretation, variable comparisons, national context, and exports. A searchable Data & Sources tab links original providers, NASA requests, and downloadable datasets. CSV and multi-sheet Excel exports support further investigation and sharing.

The intended impact is to strengthen climate literacy and make environmental evidence easier to explore and communicate. Students can investigate questions in the classroom, researchers can perform preliminary comparisons, and communities can examine records relevant to familiar places. Source links, retrieval dates, and downloadable observations help others inspect the basis of a finding.

Development used TypeScript and JavaScript, React, Tailwind CSS, and a Node.js/Express backend. Recharts supports charts, while React Simple Maps, D3, TopoJSON, and World Atlas support geographic visualization. The project integrates the NASA POWER API and optional Google Gemini API, and uses the XLSX library for spreadsheet exports. Python supported workbook inspection and data checks. Development and testing used a Windows computer and web browser, and the source code is published on GitHub.

The project’s creativity comes from connecting user questions with an interactive investigation. Users can move from a city comparison to a drawn study area, inspect differences between cells, read a calculated explanation, and follow the result back to its source. The tutorial also places city point records alongside supplied national averages, encouraging users to consider how geographic scale affects interpretation.

Design priorities included accessibility, seasonal variation, missing observations, geographic coverage, unit consistency, and API costs. The interface explains differences between national averages and point records, converts monthly rainfall totals using calendar days, and distinguishes wind measurement heights and solar sources. The current beta has identified further calibration needs in AI verification, sparse-record reliability, and several statistical edge cases.
